item.text: {"question_id":"1B.9","answer":"During 2023, Scholz’s federal government adopted a National Security Strategy that explicitly treated cyber security, civil protection, supply-chain resilience, pandemic prevention, and related risks as part of integrated security, and described the strategy as the starting point for an ongoing cross-government process (BATCH-0014-E007; BATCH-0026-E002; BATCH-0005-E009). It also enacted a smart-meter law retaining a secure-gateway framework and adding rules on data storage, deletion, and anonymization, although this was primarily an energy-digitization measure rather than a demonstrated catastrophic-dual-use safeguard (BATCH-0009-E003). Scholz personally advocated international discussion of rules for possible weaponization of generative AI, while Germany’s government supported international work on autonomous weapons, cybersecurity, and emerging technologies (BATCH-0016-E015; BATCH-0004-E004). NATO commitments involving cyber defence, biotechnology, emerging technologies, critical infrastructure, and responsible use were collective alliance commitments and do not establish Scholz’s personal authorship or German domestic implementation, funding, enforcement, or review (BATCH-0034-R10-E005). The evidence does not demonstrate that the government established and funded a comprehensive domestic framework for AI, biological, or other catastrophic dual-use risks, nor that it enforced or transparently reviewed such safeguards during the period. Important qualifications include expert findings of unresolved smart-meter security, data-privacy, capacity, staffing, and implementation problems; substantial delays and missing monitoring or security standards in digital-administration programs; privacy objections to chat-control proposals; and extensive surveillance powers that remained in force, with some legal limits proposed but not enacted (BATCH-0009-E002; BATCH-0009-E012; BATCH-0009-E024; BATCH-0009-E025;
